case_study_insert.main_stem: Keystone Haulage Link (KHL) is a cooperative in the freight forwarding and warehouse logistics sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2012 by Priya Nair, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. KHL plans to invest $640,000 in an automated warehouse sorting system with barcode scanners, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $23, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. KHL also faces staff turnover of 11% and a rising parcel mis-sort rate, and aims to improve sorting accuracy and cut complaints from its retail members.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: KHL sorted 13,500 consignments last quarter at a mis-sort rate of 2.9%, up from 2.1% a year ago. Complaints rose from 28 to 41 per month, and average dispatch time is 2.2 days. A survey of 410 retail clients found that 70% value next-day sorting and 56% would pay $1.20 more for guaranteed accuracy. A skills audit shows 16 of 55 staff need scanner training; an external barcode course costs $820 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Keystone Haulage Link for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.50 to $14.36 per hour from April 2027. (3) Packaging and fuel input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while e-commerce parcel volumes grew 6.5% in the same period.

questions.question_text: KHL is funding part of its sorting-system expansion with a seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KHL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or fixed repayments, so KHL keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $400,000 seven-year bank loan. That cash can cover fixed costs of $252,000 a year and the running of the new $640,000 sorting system while staff turnover of 11% and a 2.9% mis-sort rate are adding cost. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on scanner training or on reducing the 41 monthly complaints, helping the cooperative keep its retail members without raising the $23 selling price.

Point 2: Using $240,000 retained profit keeps control with the cooperative's members and Priya Nair's team rather than a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the barcode scanners are used. It also avoids pledging cooperative assets while the 16 staff still need $820 training and mis-sorts are rising. The survey evidence that 70% of retail clients value next-day sorting and 56% would pay $1.20 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than paid as interest that competes with the $252,000 fixed costs and the cost of the expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KHL and its financing decision.

questions.question_text: KHL is promoting its automated sorting service to retail clients. Consider a national trade exhibition, direct mail to retailers, or targeted social media and member referrals. Which should KHL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade exhibition: A stand at a logistics exhibition could introduce KHL's automated sorting to retailers from many regions and build credibility for the cooperative. However, stand, travel and staffing costs are high for a 55-employee cooperative already servicing a $400,000 loan and investing $640,000, and only a small delegate audience attends, too narrow to support 55,000 units of output. It also does not directly address the 2.9% mis-sort rate.

Direct mail to retailers: Sending details to a targeted list of retail clients can reach the exact firms that buy sorting services and can include proof of guaranteed accuracy, which 56% of the 410 surveyed clients would pay $1.20 more for. The weakness is low response rates and printing and postage costs; a leaflet cannot demonstrate the barcode scanners or explain how the 41 monthly complaints will fall.

Targeted social media and member referrals: Posts aimed at retail logistics managers, combined with referrals from KHL's own cooperative members, reach buyers who already trust the brand and can show the sorting system working. This is low cost per contact and measurable, and it lets KHL demonstrate accuracy improvements that answer the 41 complaints and the 2.2-day dispatch time, while the 70% who value next-day sorting provide a clear message.

Recommendation: KHL should choose targeted social media and member referrals. They reach the precise decision-makers, cost far less than a trade stand and convert trust in the cooperative into new contracts. The exhibition is rejected as costly and broad for a cooperative funding a $400,000 loan; direct mail is rejected as low-response and unable to demonstrate accuracy. Social media lacks the face-to-face credibility of an exhibition, so KHL should add a small presence at one regional event once the mis-sort rate is below control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KHL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of KHL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the exhibition and direct mail are rejected.

questions.question_text: KHL has staff turnover of 11% and a rising mis-sort rate. Explain two benefits for KHL of using democratic leadership within its flat structure to motivate its warehouse staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 55 employees a voice in how the 13,500 consignments are sorted, so staff can suggest practical fixes for the rise in mis-sorts from 2.1% to 2.9%. In a flat structure their ideas reach Priya Nair directly, raising ownership and job satisfaction and helping to reduce the 11% staff turnover that disrupts the new barcode system.

Point 2: Consulting staff on shift patterns and scanner routines makes the 16 workers still needing training more willing to take the $820 course, because they help shape how it is used. Involvement also helps tackle the 41 monthly complaints, as sorters who help set accuracy checks are more likely to catch errors before dispatch, protecting the 2.2-day turnaround. With a $640,000 system to run and a $400,000 loan to service, motivation that lowers turnover protects the 55,000-unit output and the 70% of clients who value next-day sorting. Democratic leadership suits a cooperative whose members expect to be consulted, though clear accuracy standards must still be enforced to bring mis-sorts down.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KHL's turnover, mis-sort rate and training needs.

questions.question_text: KHL wants to cut its 11% staff turnover and 2.9% mis-sort rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should KHL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus: Linking pay to sorting accuracy or attendance could motivate the 55 staff to push the mis-sort rate back from 2.9% toward 2.1% and improve the 2.2-day dispatch time. It is simple to understand, but the insert gives no bonus cost, so its expense cannot be calculated; it would add to fixed costs of $252,000 a year while KHL services a $400,000 loan and funds a $640,000 system. A bonus also pays after errors occur and does not change the repetitive sorting work that may be driving 11% turnover.

Job enrichment through team working: Giving warehouse staff varied tasks, shared ownership of the barcode scanners and involvement in accuracy checks makes the work more interesting and uses their local knowledge. Team checks can catch the errors behind 41 monthly complaints, and shared responsibility can reduce 11% turnover by addressing its cause. Pairing the 16 untrained staff with experienced colleagues also spreads the $820 training more effectively. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams and agree standards in a flat structure.

Decision: KHL should choose job enrichment through team working. It attacks the 11% turnover at source, can lower the 2.9% mis-sort rate and costs little next to a bonus whose size is unstated. The bonus is rejected as an expensive short-term fix that does not remove the repetitiveness behind turnover, though a small bonus could be introduced once accuracy stabilises. With no stated bonus rate the comparison is qualitative: team working changes the work itself and builds skills, while a bonus only rewards output after the event and competes with $252,000 of fixed costs and the $400,000 loan. As a cooperative, KHL's democratic culture already supports team working, so the change needs little new spending.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to KHL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of KHL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering turnover, cost, quality and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KHL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $252,000 ÷ ($23 − $9) = $252,000 ÷ $14 = 18,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 18,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $23 − $9 = $14. Answer: contribution per unit is $14.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KHL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 18,000-unit break-even output with 55,000 units sorted, giving a margin of safety of 37,000 units, so managers can see how far e-commerce volume could fall before the $640,000 system stops covering costs.
2. Use the $14 contribution per unit to test the $1.20 accuracy premium that 56% of clients would pay: raising price to $24.20 gives $15.20 contribution and lowers break-even to about 16,579 units (252,000 ÷ 15.20).
3. Average total cost is about $13.58 a unit ($252,000 ÷ 55,000 = $4.58 plus $9), below the $23 price, leaving room to absorb the 8.7% rise in packaging and fuel costs without an immediate price rise.
4. Labour productivity is 1,000 units per worker (55,000 ÷ 55), a benchmark for checking whether the $820 scanner training and team working lift output despite 11% staff turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 18,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $14 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 37,000 units; a $1.20 premium lifting contribution to $15.20 and lowering break-even to about 16,579 units; average total cost of about $13.58 against the $23 price; labour productivity of 1,000 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KHL's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has KHL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 22.5%
ROCE 2024 = 14.0%
ROCE 2025 = 16.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 840, cost of sales 504, gross profit 336; operating profit 168; capital employed 1,200. 2025 revenue 960, cost of sales 528, gross profit 432; operating profit 216; capital employed 1,350. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 336 ÷ 840 and 432 ÷ 960. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 168 ÷ 840 and 216 ÷ 960. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 168 ÷ 1,200 and 216 ÷ 1,350.

Evaluation: Every measure is higher in 2025. The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew by 120 while cost of sales rose by only 24, so the sorting operation is becoming more efficient despite the 2.9% mis-sort rate. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 1,350 of capital employed improved, which matters because KHL must service a $400,000 loan while investing $640,000 in scanners. Interest payable of 28 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 216, so financing costs are not undermining the gain. The 11% turnover and 41 monthly complaints remain risks that could reverse the trend if accuracy slips.

Conclusion: KHL's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing much faster than cost of sales. Management should use the stronger margins to fund scanner training and accuracy checks so that turnover and mis-sorts do not erase the improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether KHL improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KHL of introducing an automated warehouse sorting system with barcode scanners.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Barcode scanners can cut the mis-sort rate from 2.9% back toward 2.1% and reduce the 41 monthly complaints, which supports the survey finding that 70% of 410 retail clients value next-day sorting and 56% would pay $1.20 more for guaranteed accuracy. Better accuracy can protect the $23 selling price, the $14 contribution per unit and the 55,000-unit output, and it fits a cooperative whose members depend on reliable service.

Disadvantage: The $640,000 system adds capital that must be serviced alongside a $400,000 loan, and the 16 staff needing $820 scanner training cannot use it fully until trained, which is hard with 11% staff turnover. The insert gives no figure for scanner maintenance or software, so the exact cost saving cannot be calculated; only a qualitative comparison with the $9 variable cost is possible. If the system breaks down, the 13,500 quarterly consignments and 2.2-day dispatch promise could be disrupted, so the benefit depends on reliable operation, training and management acting on the data.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KHL's survey, accuracy and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase to $14.36 and the 8.7% rise in packaging and fuel costs will affect KHL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If KHL's $400,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year, shown as 0.0075 × $400,000. That is small against $252,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still slow the 6.5% growth in e-commerce parcel volumes.

Minimum wage increase (6.4% to $14.36 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 55,000 units ÷ 55 workers = 1,000 units per worker. If that holds, the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 11% turnover and 2.9% mis-sort rate reduce effective output, unit labour costs rise and the $14 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified here.

Input-cost inflation (8.7%): The $9 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 8.7% × $9 = $0.783, about $0.78 per unit. Across 55,000 units that is 55,000 × $0.78 = $42,900 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $14 toward about $13.22 and pushes the break-even output above 18,000 units.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in packaging and fuel costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 55,000 units and directly erodes the $14 contribution that must cover $252,000 fixed costs and service the $400,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $3,000 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. KHL can recover part of it through the $1.20 premium that 56% of retail clients accept, but rising mis-sorts already threaten service quality.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KHL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KHL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
